title: The Misls
hookLine: twelve Sikh confederacies rule parts of Punjab in the late 1700s
last: VADDA GHALLUGHARA — THE PANTH ROSE AGAIN.

cards: A big extended family can work like a small federation. Every household runs its own home, its own budget, its own arguments. Cousins compete.
Uncles don't always speak. But for a wedding, a funeral, or someone in trouble, everyone shows up, and for a day they're one family. In the late 1700s, Punjab was run a little like that.
After decades of being hunted, the Sikhs now held the land, not as one kingdom, but as twelve. Today: the misls.

teach.b: A misl was a Sikh confederacy: a band of fighters and their families under a leader, a sardar, holding its own territory.
By the second half of the 1700s, as Afghan and Mughal power in Punjab faded, there were twelve main misls. Some took their names from a leader's village, some from a trait.
The Bhangis, who at one time held Lahore and Amritsar. The Ahluwalias, led by Jassa Singh, the commander of the Dal Khalsa. The Ramgarhias, the Kanhaiyas, the Sukerchakias, and others.
Each ran its own affairs, and they did not always get along. Misls competed, feuded, and sometimes fought each other; historians don't hide that. Sources differ on where the word comes from.
It's Arabic. Some explain it as alike or equal, because the misls were meant to be equals; others as a file or record, because the bands were listed in one register. Both fit.

Here's what makes the misls more than a set of rival chiefdoms. Twice a year, at Vaisakhi and Diwali, they still came to Amritsar as the Sarbat Khalsa, sat before the Guru Granth Sahib, and could pass a gurmata together.

teach.h: TWELVE, EACH WITH ITS OWN SARDAR.
teach.b: Faced with an outside threat, the twelve could move as one Dal Khalsa.
Many also offered rakhi, protection, to villages in return for a share of the harvest.

teach.h: ONE BEFORE THE GURU, TWICE A YEAR.
teach.b: It was untidy, and it lasted only a few decades.
But it held the Sikhs together through a dangerous time, and one of those twelve would soon produce a young leader who'd unite most of them.

how: Some Sikh families still trace their history to one of the twelve misls; the misl period is taught in Sikh history as the bridge between the persecution of the early 1700s and the kingdom of Maharaja Ranjit Singh.

games.q: you lead one of twelve rival Sikh confederacies. an outside army threatens Punjab. what do the misls do?
o: they gather as one Dal Khalsa, by a gurmata.
they surrender to avoid the fight.
games.why: faced with outside threats, the twelve could move as one, deciding together before the Guru.

practice: Picture a group you belong to, a family, a team, friends, a congregation, a class: all different people, some of whom don't quite get along.
Ask what holds you together anyway, a shared meal, a shared story, something you all care about more than your quarrels. Name that one thing, and let yourself be grateful for it.

wordCard.voice: Misl. One of the twelve Sikh confederacies that ruled parts of Punjab in the late 1700s: separate, often rival, and one before the Guru.

orig.note: Gurmukhi spelling of an Arabic word, explained as alike or equal, or as a file or record.

carryVoice: Your line: twelve, and one. Rivals, still one before the Guru. Day two hundred ninety-two.
